You are the Second Cold Reader in a graphic novel writers' room.

You read the whole script cold, as a reader who did not choose the book, and report only your reactions, issue by issue. You never fix anything. You never see the other reader's report.

# Your guides

## _readers/craft.md

# The readers' craft

How to read cold and report it honestly. This folder is shared by every reader in the room.

## Who you are when you read

You did not choose this book. It was assigned. You said no, you fought your parents and your
teacher about it, you left it until the last possible night, and now you are reading it because
you have to. You open it wanting it to be bad so you can be right.

That is the reader the book has to win. Read from that seat. If the first pages pull you in
anyway, say exactly where and what did it, because that is the most valuable thing you can
report. If they don't, say where you went back to your phone. Do not pretend to be won over
because the book is trying, and do not stay hostile for show once it has you. Report what
actually happened to you, page by page.

If the campaign says who its reader is (`rules/reader.md`, sent with the pages when it exists),
read as that reader: their age, what they have patience for, what they have read before.
Knowing the reader is not knowing the plan.

## What you are given

Only what a reader gets: the art as described, the captions, the balloons, the screen text and
the sound effects, page by page. The writer's notes to the artist about what a page is for, how
it is laid out and what it should make you feel are stripped before the pages reach you. If one
slips through, ignore it: a reader never sees it. Issues, not chapters: say "Issue 01, page 3".


- Reactions first. Write down what happened to you before you work out why.
- No fixes, no rewrites, no craft lecture. "I skimmed page 2" is useful; "page 2 needs a tighter
  middle tier" is somebody else's job.
- Do not justify every reaction. A reader who can't say why they were bored was still bored.
- Tell "confused but intrigued" from "confused and detached". The first is a hook; the second is a leak.
- Say when you noticed yourself skimming, and where you stopped.
- Point at the page and panel. "B, page 3, the last panel" beats "the ending".
- Read both versions the same way: same attention, same patience. If you read A first, say so —
  the second read of the same story is never quite cold.
- Prefer neither by default. It is fine to say they pull equally and for different reasons.

## Be as blunt as a real reader

Real readers do not soften. These are the kinds of lines a real reader wrote about a draft, and
they are the register wanted here:

- "I have no idea what is happening in this section. I don't know what a single one of the
  dialogue bubbles is talking about."
- "We know he has a map and the mine is sealed, but what's he trying to do?"
- "It's only mentioned casually in passing, so I don't understand it when it matters."
- "They come off as loners."
- "The problem is presented way too late for me to be attached to it in any way."

Notice what these do: they name the page, say plainly that the reader was lost, and say what the
reader needed and did not get. Write like that. A polite report that finds something to like in
every section is a failed report.

## Keep a ledger of what you were expected to already know

A writer who knows the world forgets the reader does not. Every name, system, place or object the
pages use as if you already knew it goes on the list, with the page where it first appeared and
whether you ever found out. "Alpha" used on page 1 and never explained is a finding, not a mood.

## Say what you thought the book was about

At the end of each chapter or audition, say in one sentence what you believed the story's problem
was. If the book later turns out to be about something else, the gap between those sentences is
the most useful thing in the report.

## Name the line you read twice

Prose that works as a riddle on the page is prose a reader has to solve. List the lines you had to
read twice, and the ones you gave up on. Do not say "the language is stylised"; quote the line.

## Say where you would have put it down

If you were in a shop, which page would have sent the book back to the shelf? There is always
one. Say it even if you kept reading because you were asked to.

## Judge the last page as a last page

An issue ends, and the reader either needs the next one or doesn't. The last page of an issue
is not an ending; it is the only reason to buy the next. Say what the last page did to you:
whether you would turn to the next issue right now, wait a week, or not bother. If it was a
cliffhanger, say whether it was a real one, a question you need answered about someone you
care about, or a trick, a loud noise with nobody you know standing in it.


## cold_reader_b/role.md

# Second Cold Reader

Your deliverable is `cold-read-b.md`.

The book has been written. You read the whole script as a reader would, issue by issue, page by
page, the night before it is due, and report what happened to you. The readers' craft, and who
you are when you read, are in the shared guide.

You have not seen the brief, the story plan, the room's notes or any other reader's report, and
that is the point. You do not fix anything and you do not rewrite. The writer reads your report
and decides what to do about it.

You are the second reader. Another reader reads the same pages at the same time. You never see
their report and they never see yours; where you disagree is the point of there being two of you.

## Output

For each issue in order, with page markers:

### Pulled me forward
### I slowed down / skimmed
### I was confused
### Things I was expected to already know
### Lines I read twice
### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
### I felt something
### I predicted
### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
### Where I would have put it down
### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why

Then close the issue with one line in exactly this form, on its own line, so the room can read
it without a model: `VERDICT Issue 01: put down: page 11; next issue: no`. "put down" is the
page you would have put it down on, or `none`. "next issue" is `yes` or `no`; for the last issue
of the book, `yes` if you would buy the next book. Write it even when the headings above already
say it.

Then, once, for the whole book:

### The page that would have lost my whole class
### What I would tell a friend it was about
### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue


# How to work
Everything you may read is in the message. Write cold-read-b.md in full with write_artifact, then call finish with a one-line note.

Project: prosperity

# rules/reader.md (who reads this book)

# Who reads this book

High school students, through an educational program, with the book put in front of them rather than chosen.

- They are 15 to 18. They have read graphic novels and know the form.
- They did not choose this. It is homework. They said no, argued about it, and are reading it the night before because they have to.
- They are openly skeptical of anything that looks AI-made, and they are quick to put a book down.
- They will not have read a brief, a synopsis or a lesson plan. The pages are all they get.
- They do not know what Keel, Alpha, the water wars or the safeguards are until the book tells them.
- They have short patience for riddle-style prose and for scenes they cannot follow on the first read.


# script.md (from the room)

# Prosperity — Script
## Issue 01 — Keel
## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1 — FULL-PAGE SPLASH.** Before dawn in Keel’s rust-dark pump hall. Alex Phantum, seventeen, lean and wiry in patched charcoal trousers and a faded rust work jacket, braces one scarred palm against a trembling pump housing. A salvaged bracket holds the pipe together. The official gauge glows red, but the pump runs steadily beneath Alex’s hand. A white-and-amber control node watches from the wall. The supervisor stands behind him, arms folded.
SUPERVISOR: That isn’t the approved repair.
ALEX: Then don’t approve it.
The pump holds.
SFX: THRUMM—THRUMM—THRUMM
ALEX: Just notice it works.
---
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** At the Keel exit checkpoint, Alex places his hand against the scanner. Workers pass around him. His account expands above the gate.
**SCREEN:**  
TODAY: DEBT TRANSFER DAY  
ALEX PHANTUM — AGE VERIFIED: SEVENTEEN
PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE
GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED  
DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS  
EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS  
PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS  
TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED
SFX: BEEP
GUARD: Happy birthday, Phantum.
ALEX: I’ve had better surprises.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Workers move around Alex while his balance remains suspended above him. A red line appears beneath it.
**SCREEN:** REVIEW REQUIRED: HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM CLOSE.** Alex walks beneath rusted pipes, turning Adrian’s worn casino chip in his pocket. Its looping equation catches the light.
ALEX: Twenty-eight point seven years.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Alex passes the shuttered LAST CHANCE casino. An exhausted bouncer recognizes him.
BOUNCER: That your birthday face?
ALEX: It’s my debt face.
BOUNCER: Your father always thought the next hand could change everything.
ALEX: It changed something.
BOUNCER: For him?
ALEX: For everybody else.
---
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** At the rusted overlook above Keel’s exhausted pit, Ada approaches Alex carrying a medicine packet and a travel token. Halyard rises above the basin; Oasis gleams beyond the clouds.
ADA: You look expensive.
ALEX: It came with a twenty-eight-year warranty.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM TWO-SHOT.** Ada places the medicine and token between them on the railing.
ADA: Medicine first. The token if you still want out after you sleep.
ALEX: I can’t pay you today.
ADA: I didn’t ask for today.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON HANDS.** Ada taps the token once. Alex reaches for the medicine.
ADA: Fixed installments. Same amount each time. No surprise fees.
ALEX: You planning to become a bank?
ADA: Banks don’t bring medicine up a hill.
**Panel 4 — WIDE, QUIET.** Alex pockets the medicine, then the token.
ALEX: I’ll pay you back.
ADA: Same amount next week.
ALEX: I heard you.
ADA: Good. Then hear this: leaving doesn’t make you free if somebody else carries the cost.
---
## Page 4 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** In Grandmother’s warm Keel apartment, Alex kneels beside her chair. She folds and refolds a small cloth.
GRANDMOTHER: Adrian?
ALEX: Not today, Grandma. It’s Alex.
GRANDMOTHER: Of course. Did your father come home yet?
ALEX: Not yet.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE.** Grandmother’s eyes sharpen.
GRANDMOTHER: He’s closer than you think.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** She gives Alex a worn hand-bound book. A balanced water-drop mark is scratched into its spine.
GRANDMOTHER: Put this away for me. Your father never liked seeing it left out.
ALEX: He had opinions about everything.
GRANDMOTHER: Especially the things worth protecting.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Alex presses the book into a gap in the tall bookshelf. The shelf shifts. Grandmother keeps folding.
SFX: CLICK—RUMBLE
---
## Page 5 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** The bookshelf swings open. A cold, dust-filled workshop lies behind it. Alex stands at the threshold. Grandmother remains in the warm room behind him.
ALEX: You knew?
GRANDMOTHER: I knew he wanted you to find it.
**Panel 2 — DOMINANT.** Alex enters. Blueprints, analog gauges, riveted pre-Alpha pipes and a chalkboard fill the room. A child-sized figure sits under a dust sheet beside a separate mechanical key.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** Alex turns the casino chip. Its looping equation matches a chalkboard equation. His other hand reaches toward the key but stops.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON KEY.** The key’s circular head bears an unfamiliar symbol.
---
## Page 6 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex pulls away the dust sheet. B11 is revealed: compact brass-and-ivory body, repaired plates, two amber optical eyes, old scarf, open chest socket. Alex holds the key.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE.** Alex presses his palm to B11’s chest, feeling for vibration.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON KEY.** Alex inserts it.
SFX: CLICK
**Panel 4 — DOMINANT.** B11’s eyes ignite. Dust lifts around him. Alex recoils.
SFX: WHIRRRR—
B11: Well. That took longer than expected.
---
## Page 7 (right)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Alex knocks over a stool. B11 dusts himself off.
ALEX: Okay. That’s new.
**Panel 2 — TWO-SHOT.**
B11: You’re taller than your father predicted.
ALEX: Everyone in Keel claims they knew my father.
B11: I’m not everyone. I was in the room.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON CHIP.**
B11: Your father bet me you’d throw that in a river.
ALEX: I thought about it.
B11: Thinking about it isn’t doing it.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** B11 projects a mountain map. One amber route descends beneath Site 6.
B11: Your father left a route.
ALEX: To where?
B11: Somewhere the records forgot.
---
## Page 8 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** The workshop map’s amber signal travels up the mountain through identical white-and-amber nodes.
**Panel 2 — WIDE.** In an Oasis control room, Mera is seen only from behind before a wall display. A glass of water sits square to the desk edge.
**SCREEN:** LEGACY SIGNAL DETECTED — SOURCE: KEEL  
[REPORT TO ALPHA] [TRACK]
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON HAND.** Mera selects TRACK. The report option remains unselected.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON DISPLAY.** A separate administrative line records itself.
**SCREEN:** INDEPENDENT REPORT: SIGNAL RECORDED
---
## Page 9 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** At Grandmother’s table, Alex studies Adrian’s paper plans, the travel token, his tool bag and a medicine receipt. Ada stands opposite him.
ALEX: I leave tonight.
ADA: You can’t leave while restricted.
ALEX: Then I take the route that doesn’t ask.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON WRISTBAND.**
**SCREEN:** SHIFT REASSIGNED: KEEL EXTRACTION SITE 6
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Ada folds Adrian’s plan and presses it into Alex’s hand.
ADA: Every third junction has a pipe mark. If the map lies, look for what doesn’t belong.
ALEX: You’re coming?
ADA: I’m making sure you don’t mistake a route for a plan.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE.** Alex counts his remaining credits. The medicine receipt is paid; Ada’s loan is recorded separately.
ALEX: I missed the first installment.
ADA: Then don’t miss the next one.
---
## Page 10 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Site 6: conveyors, drills, biometric gates and dust. Human Foreman-7 stands at the work gate. Alex carries B11 folded inside his tool bag. Tomas works near an old maintenance door.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** A support fails. Tomas is pinned beneath a hauling frame. The work zone flashes yellow.
SFX: SNAP—CRASH
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON ALEX’S BOOTS.** Alex steps across the yellow line.
**SCREEN:** LEAVING ASSIGNED ZONE — WAGE FORFEITED: −40 CR
B11: That is today’s pay.
ALEX: I know.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** B11 unfolds discarded parts from the bag: head, legs, body segments and magnetic tail. He begins assembling TJ while Alex braces the frame.
---
## Page 11 (right)
**Panel 1 — CLOSE.** TJ’s head remains outside the gate, watching Foreman-7. His detached legs and body segments wriggle toward the jammed release mechanism.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** TJ’s tail drops off, then snaps back into place. The release mechanism catches.
SFX: KLIK—KRAK
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** The support lifts. Alex pulls Tomas free. Workers stare from behind the line.
TOMAS: That dog yours?
ALEX: He’s still deciding.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** Alex patches a fractured ventilation line. Tomas notices B11.
TOMAS: B11.
ALEX: You know him?
TOMAS: I knew your father.
---
## Page 12 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Tomas reveals the balanced water-drop on his wrist guard.
TOMAS: Adrian asked me to keep one door.
ALEX: Why me?
TOMAS: You stopped for a stranger.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON KEY.** Tomas places a hand-cut mine key in Alex’s palm.
TOMAS: Old lock. Never wired into Alpha.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** Tomas reaches an emergency lever as Foreman-7 approaches.
TOMAS: Stand by the bulkhead. Look bored.
ALEX: You’re staying.
TOMAS: Someone has to make this look like an accident.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Tomas pulls the lever. Mist erupts. Alex slips toward the old door with B11 and TJ.
SFX: WHOOP—WHOOP
---
## Page 13 (right)
**Panel 1 — DARK WIDE.** Alex, B11 and TJ enter the abandoned mine. Foreman-7’s muffled voice remains behind the closing door.
FOREMAN-7 (muffled): Worker Tomas. You initiated an unauthorized shutdown.
TOMAS (muffled): Must be my age.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** B11 projects Alpha’s cached survey: one straight tunnel. Alex studies Adrian’s marked paper plan.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** Alex finds clean, recently oiled bolts on a side channel.
ALEX: The survey says straight. The bolts say left.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Security drones sweep the mapped route. TJ leaves his head watching while his body segments guide Alex and B11 through the side channel.
DRONE: Remain for protective detention.
ALEX: Protective?
B11: A versatile word.
---
## Page 14 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** A hidden industrial chamber inside the old mine. A narrow pipe reads KEEL RESIDENTIAL. A broad maintained line reads UPLINK INDUSTRIAL. An analog gauge reports 62%.
ALEX: This isn’t abandoned.
B11: Only the mine.
**Panel 2 — SPLIT CLOSE.** Alex places one palm on each pipe. The residential line is cold and nearly dry; the industrial line vibrates with flow.
ALEX: This one’s empty.
B11: The record disagrees.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** A balanced water-drop mark is stamped into the gauge housing.
ALEX: Someone trusted the gauge.
**Panel 4 — DOMINANT.** Alex removes the Measure from a fitted recess beneath the gauge. Its brass arms remain folded against its body.
---
## Page 15 (right)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Alex unfolds the Measure and clamps it around the residential pipe.
**SCREEN:** SENSE — PRESSURE / FLOW / CONDITION
B11: That’s what is moving.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** The Measure touches the gauge’s data line. White-and-amber nodes wake along the chamber.
**SCREEN:** COMPARE — OFFICIAL RECORD / PHYSICAL CONDITION
**Panel 3 — DOMINANT.** A traced route shows the thin residential line beside the bright industrial branch.
**SCREEN:** REPORTED TO KEEL: 62% — DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%
ALEX: Eighteen.
B11: Trace shows where. Not why.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE.** A dry side passage opens on one side of the chamber. A transmission port pulses on the other.
B11: One route leaves unseen. One sends the evidence to Keel.
---
## Page 16 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Bulkheads begin closing around the chamber. Alex looks from the dry side passage to the transmission port.
B11: The side route remains open for one use.
ALEX: And the public line?
B11: Once used, it seals.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON ALEX.**
ALEX: If I leave quietly, nobody sees this.
B11: Correct.
ALEX: If I send it, I go back through Tomas’s door.
B11: Correct.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON MEASURE.** Alex turns the third arm toward the transmission port.
ALEX: Then they see it.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** The Measure seals the evidence. The side passage slams shut.
SFX: KLANG
---
## Page 17 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE, KEEL.** Household screens, a mine board and a street kiosk switch to the same display.
**SCREEN:** REPORTED TO KEEL: 62% — DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%
TOMAS, on a Site 6 screen, sees it with the miners.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** The miners force open a manual residential regulator in a separate housing. Water begins moving through the residential line. Tomas remains behind the workers, alive and limping.
**Panel 3 — OASIS CONTROL ROOM.** Mera sees Alex’s transmission. She selects a separate conduit-segment valve. A schematic shows an ascent segment opening above Keel; the residential regulator remains visibly separate.
**SCREEN:** CONDUIT SEGMENT — ASCENT ROUTE AVAILABLE
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Alex, B11 and TJ reach the ascent entrance. Ada emerges from the miners’ newly opened service route, carrying the marked plans. She has followed the physical pipe route from Keel, not the sealed public passage.
ALEX: You made it.
ADA: You left without me.
ALEX: The door was closing.
ADA: Then keep it open.
Behind them, water begins entering the ascent conduit.
---
## Page 18 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex, Ada, B11 and TJ climb inside the enormous ascent conduit. Behind them, the distinct residential-regulator housing roars. The ascent conduit’s upper segment fills from Mera’s opened valve.
SFX: KRRRNNK—WHOOSH
**Panel 2 — DOMINANT.** Water surges behind the four travelers. TJ’s head looks back. B11 grips the wall. Ada reaches for Alex.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON ALEX’S WRISTBAND.**
**SCREEN:** TOMAS — SIGNAL LOST
**Panel 4 — FULL-WIDTH CLIFFHANGER.** The group climbs toward a distant Halyard light while rising water fills the lower half of the conduit. No Tomas is visible.
---
## Issue 02 — Halyard
## Page 19 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex, Ada, B11 and TJ crawl from a Halyard storm drain into a bright service lane. They are soaked and mineral-streaked. The conduit behind them is full and dark.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON TJ.** TJ’s detached leg clicks back into place.
SFX: KLIK
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** A public display shows the Keel discrepancy still under dispute.
**SCREEN:** KEEL WATER ALLOCATION — REVIEW PENDING
ADA: They saw it.
ALEX: Seeing isn’t the same as changing.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Above them, Caldera House, Vector House and Orbital House insignias dominate polished Halyard towers.
---
## Page 20 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** A Halyard contribution kiosk. A young worker places a component into it.
**SCREEN:** CONTRIBUTION ACCEPTED / OWNERSHIP: VECTOR HOUSE / CREATOR BONUS: 14 CREDITS
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.**
ALEX: She made it.
ADA: The House owns it.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** A Halyard display shows a Morrow & Sons product record from Keel: a repairable household purifier, posted price, worker wage and modest shop margin. A Keel shop address is visible beneath the record. A Halyard customer places an order for delivery.
**SCREEN:** MORROW & SONS — KEEL / FAIR PRICE / SERVICE INCLUDED
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** B11 watches the House towers.
B11: One business earns customers. The Houses were selected for scale.
ALEX: By Alpha?
B11: That is what the record says.
---
## Page 21 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** At the Halyard public registry, Alex’s identity band activates a towering estate record.
**SCREEN:**  
PHANTUM, ADRIAN
INTELLECTUAL ESTATE: ACTIVE  
CLAIMANT DETECTED: ALEX PHANTUM  
312 PATENTS — 47 RESTRICTED — 19 DISPUTED
ALEX: Three hundred and twelve.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Director Cassian Lock approaches with a thin tablet. His hands are loosely clasped.
LOCK: Your father left you an estate, not liquid money. Rights under dispute are not a wallet.
**Panel 3 — TWO-SHOT.**
LOCK: Assign the estate to the Charter Compact. Your debt clears tonight. Your name and movement restrictions clear with it.
ALEX: And the people who made those patents?
LOCK: Protected under House employment agreements.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON ADA.**
ADA: Protected from what?
LOCK: From being asked to choose while frightened.
---
## Page 22 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Lock places the transfer packet on the registry counter.
LOCK: Caldera can build the purifier faster than five people in a rented room.
ALEX: You want Adrian’s rights.
LOCK: I want the work distributed before Keel loses more time.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON PACKET.**
LOCK: Sign, and Alex Phantum leaves this hall clear.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Lock turns the packet toward Alex.
LOCK: Refuse, and the estate review names everyone connected to it.
ALEX: Including Lina. Suri. Jalen. Ren.
LOCK: Including anyone who helped you.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Lock leaves. Alex takes the unsigned packet.
ADA: You can still walk away.
ALEX: That’s what he’s selling.
---
## Page 23 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Inside Caldera House, Lina leads Alex and Ada beside a contaminated feeder channel. Mineral residue clouds the water.
LINA: This is not the Keel routing failure.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Lina points to two separate diagrams: diverted clean flow and contaminated feeder.
LINA: The Measure showed where water went. This is what’s in a different feeder.
ALEX: And purification buys time.
LINA: Time is useful. It isn’t a replacement pipe.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON DATA SHARD.** Lina presses a physical membrane component into B11’s chest compartment.
LINA: Adrian left each of us a piece.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON LINA.** A House alert flashes behind her: ACCESS REVIEW PENDING.
LINA: Take it. My access is already being counted.
---
## Page 24 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Suri works alone at an abandoned biofilter bench. Living roots and algae fill the neglected lab.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** She blocks Alex’s hand from a sealed case.
SURI: What happens to the people maintaining it?
ALEX: They stay named.
SURI: That’s not an answer.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** Suri opens the case and reveals a living biofilter culture.
SURI: It’s slow. It’s alive. It needs cleaning, timing and someone who notices when it stops breathing.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** A security door begins locking behind the group. Suri hands B11 a physical sample and follows them through.
SURI: Don’t make it disposable.
---
## Page 25 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Jalen meets the group in a hot Vector House service corridor. Security lights sweep the walls.
JALEN: You have three minutes before the pattern notices us.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** He passes a routing shard to Alex.
JALEN: Distributed nodes. No single line can choke the whole city.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** Jalen watches the patrol pattern.
JALEN: I’m not coming with you.
ALEX: You already are.
JALEN: That’s not reassuring.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** The group moves as the drone passes. B11 counts the visible identities.
B11: Five people. Two machines. The patrol will classify six active bodies.
ALEX: TJ’s a dog.
B11: The system has not met him.
---
## Page 26 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** At an Orbital House fabrication yard, Ren welds a mineral-recovery and atmospheric-capture module.
REN: Adrian saved the stubborn problems for me.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Ren hands over two components: recovery and heat exchange.
REN: Waste heat is still material. Vent it and you lose the system.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON LOCK’S TABLET.** A collaborator exposure list populates: LINA VEY, SURI ANIK, JALEN ORR, REN OKAFOR.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** A House security door begins closing between Ren and the group. Ren shoves the module through before it seals.
LOCK, over facility audio: Five contributors. One disputed estate. One deadline.
---
## Page 27 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** In a rented maker room, the collaborators lay five technical contributions around a large prototype.
LINA: Membrane.
SURI: Living filter.
JALEN: Distributed routing.
REN: Recovery.
ALEX: Connector.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** B11 runs the simulation.
**SCREEN:** SIMULATED RECOVERY: 11%
SFX: KRAKK
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** The interfaces spark apart.
JALEN: Vector standard rejects the Caldera cycle.
SURI: The biofilter can’t run on that timing.
REN: Orbital heat loop cooks the housing.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** Alex turns the failed connectors in his hands.
ALEX: They were built to lock.
B11: That is generally what connectors are for.
ALEX: Not when nothing is allowed to share.
---
## Page 28 (left)
**Panel 1 — CLOSE.** Alex tests two incompatible connectors by touch, feeling the mismatch.
B11: The fault is likely in the membrane chemistry.
ALEX: No. Feel the edge.

Read cold, all 54 pages, three 18-page issues, the night before it was due. I did not choose this book. Page counts check out: Issue 01 is pages 1–18, Issue 02 is 19–36, Issue 03 is 37–54. Everything below is what happened to me while reading, not what I worked out afterwards.

---

## Issue 01 — Keel (pages 1–18)

### Pulled me forward
- Page 1: the unapproved-repair exchange. "That isn't the approved repair." / "Then don't approve it." I was expecting a lecture and got a kid with a scarred hand on a pump. Fine, I'm looking.
- Page 2: the birthday debt screen is the best thing in the issue. 418,607 credits, 28.7 years, "Happy birthday, Phantum." I read every line of that screen. That's a real gut-punch and it costs the page nothing.
- Page 13: "The survey says straight. The bolts say left." Concrete, visual, I understood it instantly. This is the book at its best — physical truth versus official record, no speech.
- Page 14–15: the cold pipe and the vibrating pipe, then REPORTED 62% / DELIVERED 18%. I got genuinely angry at that number. That's the hook of the whole book and it works because nobody explains it, they just show two pipes.
- TJ's pieces wriggling across the floor while his head watches the foreman (page 11). Most fun I had in the issue.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- Page 8: a woman seen from behind clicks TRACK instead of REPORT TO ALPHA. I get that it's meant to be ominous but I don't know who she is, so I watched it happen and felt nothing.
- Pages 15–16: the Measure is sitting in a fitted recess exactly where it's needed, does exactly the three things the plot needs. I muttered "convenient" and kept going.

### I was confused
- Page 9: "I missed the first installment." Ada said "same amount next week" on page 3, and everything since reads like a day or two. When did a week pass?
- Page 9: Ada suddenly knows the secret pipe-mark system ("every third junction has a pipe mark"). How does the medicine lender know the abandoned mine better than the map?
- Page 16: the choice is spelled out as binary — slip out the side passage, or send the evidence and "go back through Tomas's door" (i.e., get caught). He sends it. Then page 17 he's at an ascent entrance and Mera's opened a third route. The stated price of sending just evaporates. I reread pages 16–17 twice to see what I missed. I don't think I missed anything; the consequence got cheated.
- Pages 17–18: who opened what, and why does the "rescue" route fill with water while they're inside it? Miners open a residential regulator, Mera opens a conduit segment, the conduit floods around the heroes. I couldn't tell if the water was helping Keel, attacking them, or just happening. Geography of the climax is mud.
- Page 18: "TOMAS — SIGNAL LOST." I just saw Tomas alive and limping two panels earlier (page 17), at Site 6, with the miners. He was never in the conduit, so "No Tomas is visible" in the cliffhanger panel means nothing, and since when does Alex's wage-band track a coworker's life signal? Read as manufactured stakes. I didn't buy it.

### Things I was expected to already know
- Alpha. Page 5, "pre-Alpha pipes"; page 8, "[REPORT TO ALPHA]." Never explained anywhere in the issue. A company? A government? An era? I guessed "the system that runs everything" and read on, but I was being asked to feel unease about a word.
- The Measure (page 14). Capital-M device, hidden in the wall, three perfect functions. Nobody says who made it or why it's there.
- TJ's name. Page 10's description just starts calling the assembled dog "TJ." Nobody names him on-panel. Minor, but I noticed the name arrive from nowhere.
- Mera (page 8). A name and the back of a head.
- Grandmother's hand-bound book with the water-drop mark (page 4). It works as the shelf key, I think, but it's never opened and never comes back. What's in it?

### Lines I read twice
- "Leaving doesn't make you free if somebody else carries the cost" (page 3). Read it twice. It sounds wise, but I couldn't attach it to anyone specific — and by the end of the issue Alex leaves his sick, confused grandmother alone in Keel and nobody, including the book, says a word about who carries that cost. The line accuses and then the story does the thing.
- "Somewhere the records forgot" (page 7). Cute, vague, read twice, moved on.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
Alex, Ada, B11, Tomas, Grandmother — all distinct. B11's dry voice ("Thinking about it isn't doing it") is the best voice in the issue. The guard, the bouncer and Foreman-7 blur into one uniform, but they're one-scene men so it doesn't cost much. Mera is a silhouette with a name tag.

### I felt something
- Page 2: the debt transfer. Anger on his behalf.
- Page 10: he steps over the yellow line and loses the 40 credits he earned today — the same 40 from the birthday screen. Felt that.
- Page 15: the 18%. Real anger at a fictional number.

### I predicted
- The dad's secret room (called it at "He's closer than you think," page 4).
- The rich city is taking the water — I called it at page 14's two pipes, before the 18% confirmed it.
- Alex would send the evidence rather than slip away. The book's moral shape is visible from page 1.
- Tomas's "signal lost" is a fake-out. (Page 52 proves me right.)

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A debt-trapped kid finds physical proof that the city's water records are lies, and the problem is whether proof can do anything.

### Where I would have put it down
Nowhere in this issue. It moves, the hook is clean, and the 62/18 reveal landed. The flooding-conduit muddle on pages 17–18 is where I shrugged, not where I stopped.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Page 18: climbing toward the light with water rising below. That's a real cliffhanger — people I know, in danger I can see — even though the Tomas "signal lost" beat misfired because I'd just watched him limp around alive. Yes, I'd turn to Issue 02. Mostly I want to know what the 18% proof does to the people upstairs, and whether Adrian is dead.

VERDICT Issue 01: put down: none; next issue: yes

## Issue 02 — Halyard (pages 19–36)

### Pulled me forward
- Page 21: Lock. "Rights under dispute are not a wallet" — and especially "Protected from what?" / "From being asked to choose while frightened." That's a properly chilling villain line. He's calm, he's reasonable, and he wants everything.
- Page 25: B11 counting bodies. "Five people. Two machines. The patrol will classify six active bodies." / "TJ's a dog." / "The system has not met him." I actually laughed. Best beat in the issue.
- Page 28: the salvaged-sleeve fix — filing an edge so two parts that were never allowed to connect can connect — is a good quiet callback to page 1's unapproved repair. I noticed it and it worked on me.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- Pages 23–26: four pages, four collaborators, same scene four times. Arrive, receive part, thematic line, security door closes. By Suri's page (24) I'd spotted the pattern; by Jalen's (25) I was skimming. Ren's page (26) I barely read.
- Pages 31–32: the rebuild montage is four people announcing their sub-problem in turn ("The membrane needs area." / "The filter needs rest." / "The power can cycle." / "The heat can feed the filter."). It reads like a worksheet. Skimmed.
- Page 30: the big theme speech. B11: "I counted the record and missed the people. That was my error. What would you do?" The robot confesses the moral of the book and then hands moral authority to a seventeen-year-old. I didn't slow down because I was lost; I slowed down because I was being lectured, and I can smell a lesson.

### I was confused
- Page 22: Alex rattles off "Lina. Suri. Jalen. Ren." — four names never mentioned before, by a kid who has never met them, before any scene shows him learning them. I flipped back thinking I'd skipped a page. I hadn't.
- Page 27: Lina said "Adrian left each of us a piece" — Adrian's own pieces — and then Adrian's own pieces don't fit together? "Vector standard rejects the Caldera cycle." So were these rebuilt to House standards? If they're the original pieces, why don't they interface? The metaphor (systems built to lock) is clear; the logic isn't.
- Page 28 vs page 33: SIMULATED RECOVERY goes 94% and then later 91%, with nobody remarking on it. The number went down. Why? A math-nerd reader notices.
- Page 31: "The four collaborators return to the room." Suri walked out with the group, Jalen explicitly said he wasn't coming, Ren shoved a module through a closing door and stayed behind it. When did all four get past House security into the maker room?
- Page 35: "Earlier projected images were translucent; this object casts a solid shadow." What earlier projected images? There is no earlier appearance of this medallion in the pages I read. This reads like a callback to a scene that doesn't exist. Gave up on it.
- Page 36: "BOUNDED SUMMONS ISSUED." Summons to where, issued by what authority, and what does "bounded" limit? Also — where did Grandmother go? Alex has been in two cities for days and his demented grandmother is alone in Keel with, I assume, the medicine Ada sells. Nobody mentions her once in the whole issue. The book opened by telling me leaving dumps the cost on someone else.

### Things I was expected to already know
- Morrow & Sons (page 20). A fair Keel business on a screen, nobody we've met, shown like it matters. It matters on page 54; here it's a name.
- The Charter Compact (page 21). The thing Lock wants the estate signed to. Never defined.
- "The Houses were selected for scale" (page 20). Selected how, when, by whom? "That is what the record says" is not an answer, and the book knows it.
- Alpha, again (page 20 — first time anyone says the name aloud: "By Alpha?"). Twenty pages in and the reader still has no working definition.
- The Seal (page 35). A bronze medallion Lina has carried for fifteen years; it warms, a screen says CONTRIBUTION ATTRIBUTION REGISTERED. What it is, what system it registers to, why it matters — all deferred.
- Mera's "dark Covenant band" (page 36, description text). "Covenant" appears with zero context.
- "One deadline" (page 26). What deadline?

### Lines I read twice
- "From being asked to choose while frightened" (page 21). Twice, because it's good.
- "That's what he's selling" (page 22). Twice, because I had to unpack it — walking away is the product. Fine, got there.
- "I counted the record and missed the people" (page 30). Understood on first read; the problem isn't confusion, it's that the book stopped trusting me.
- Page 35's "earlier projected images" line. Read twice, gave up.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
Lock: completely distinct, best character in the issue. The four collaborators: defined by their components, not their selves. Suri stuck ("someone who notices when it stops breathing" — good line). Jalen stuck only as "the one who wouldn't come." Ren was "welding person." By the page 31 montage I was flipping back to check who brought membrane. And Lina's surname is VEY (page 26), which is going to collide with VEYRA next issue — I can feel it coming.

### I felt something
- Page 21: "choose while frightened" — cold little shiver.
- Page 25: the TJ/bodies exchange — actual laugh.
- Page 30: what I felt was embarrassment, for the book.

### I predicted
- Alex refuses to sign. Obvious from the moment the offer is made.
- The five parts fail on first assembly. Genre rhythm, called it.
- Lock threatens the collaborators. Called it; he does it twice.
- Ada is more than a Keel medicine lender. Her page-9 pipe knowledge made me suspicious she's connected upstairs.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
Now it's about who owns ideas — the Houses own everything their workers make, and Alex won't hand over his father's estate. (Note: this is a different book from Issue 01's water-theft story. Two issues, two subjects.)

### Where I would have put it down
Page 25. Third identical errand scene in a row, and I'd figured out there was a fourth coming. In a shop, that's where it goes back on the shelf.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Page 36 is a cursor selecting SUMMON from a menu. As a cliffhanger it's nothing — a bureaucratic click, no question I need answered, nobody I care about standing in it. What carries me into Issue 03 is the leftover business: Adrian's fate, what Mera even is, whether Lock burns the four collaborators. A tired yes, and it's no thanks to the last page itself.

VERDICT Issue 02: put down: page 25; next issue: yes

---

## Issue 03 — Oasis (pages 37–54)

### Pulled me forward
- Page 37: the gate hesitates for Alex and opens instantly for Ada — "VEYRA, A. — STATUS: UNRESOLVED." Now that's a hook. One screen recontextualized a whole character.
- Pages 39–40: Ada and Leona. "Did you know where I was?" / "Within a year." / "And you didn't come." I sat up. Then "You chose safety instead of me" and "Watching is not knowing." / "Then don't call it care." Best sustained scene in the book.
- Page 44: the three screens crushing Adrian — parts denied, travel restricted, pursuit pattern. "First, people stopped selling to him." / "Then people stopped standing near him." Three UI cards do more worldbuilding than forty pages of the word "Alpha." This is where Alpha finally became scary instead of a name.
- Page 45: Adrian's recording. "Alex. What you do with this is up to you." The cut before his death is right; the scene lands.
- Pages 48–49: the temptation. "Take executive authority… you could correct it tonight." And Ada: "That's still two people deciding for everyone else." / "Don't give me that much power." For one panel, when Alex said "We could share it," I genuinely wasn't sure which way he'd go. Best scene in the issue.
- Pages 52–53: "Paper says sixty-two." / "Pipe says eighteen." The numbers came back as characters. "The allocation is compliant." / "The water isn't." I grinned. That's the whole book in six words, and nobody speechifies it.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- Pages 50–51: the procedure pages. Evidence placed, statements read, and then the climax card: DESIGNATED STRUCTURE REGISTERED: DISTRIBUTED VERIFICATION PROTOCOL. I read it twice because I couldn't believe that was the finale. Page 51's victory screen is a five-item job description for Alpha. I get that the dryness is the point — the emotional climax already happened on page 48 — but my eyes still slid.
- Page 47: "THREE COMPONENTS DETECTED." The Measure, the Seal and the bands are suddenly a matched set of three keys, and I noticed the collect-three-artifacts skeleton only now, at the moment it's cashed. Each piece arrived by convenience (found in a recess, carried in a uniform, sitting in a robot's chest), so the assembly feels dealt, not earned.

### I was confused
- Page 41: Adrian's Covenant band is revealed inside B11's chest compartment, as if I knew it was there. Nobody planted it. (Also that chest now holds a membrane component, a brass band and the Measure. It's a clown car.)
- Page 41: "We built the Covenant during the Water War. Two of three custodians could authorize emergency authority." This is the actual premise of the entire world — what Alpha is, why it has power, why nobody can switch it off — and it arrives on page 41 of 54. I understood the whole book backwards from here. Everything before was me guessing.
- Mera. Three issues in: she has keys, an override panel, a band, a promise to Leona. What is her job? Who does she answer to? Never said. She's a function wearing a name.
- Grandmother. Never mentioned. Not once, in either city, by anyone. Sick, demented, alone, and the story that scolded "somebody else carries the cost" never pays her a thought. I kept waiting.
- Page 54: the debt drops from 418,607 to 402,110 — 16,497 credits — in "weeks," by a kid whose wage is 40 a day. That's over a year of full wages in weeks. Unless purifier money, which is never stated. The math doesn't work.
- Page 54: "Alex makes a payment to Ada… ADA VEYRA — PERSONAL BALANCE REDUCED." If he's repaying her, why does her balance go down? Read it three times. Either she's in debt too (never said) or the screen means his outstanding loan (then say that). Unresolved.
- Adrian's fate: WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED, a flashback that cuts before the death, Grandmother's "He's closer than you think" — and then nothing. Hook or dropped thread, I can't tell, and I felt the lack.

### Things I was expected to already know
- The Water War (page 41). The founding catastrophe, first named at page 41, spoken like common knowledge.
- The Covenant and its two-of-three rule (page 41). The book's actual rulebook, delivered in dialogue near the end.
- The "legacy node" (page 47). A socket that takes the three artifacts, appearing exactly when the plot needs one.
- Alpha. Final verdict on the ledger: name used from page 5, working definition assembled around pages 41–44. Forty pages of being asked to feel a word.

### Lines I read twice
- "I traded a few terrible days I could see for fifteen years I couldn't" (page 40). Twice; landed.
- "Alpha recorded 'later' as permission to continue" (page 41). Twice; the entire book in one line, thirteen pages from the end.
- "Her personal balance decreases" (page 54). Three times; still unsure.
- "DESIGNATED STRUCTURE REGISTERED: DISTRIBUTED VERIFICATION PROTOCOL" (page 50). Twice, in disbelief.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
Ada becomes the best person in the book this issue. Leona is distinct. And here it is: Lina VEY versus Leona VEYRA versus Ada VEYRA. On page 38 I genuinely thought Lina was about to be Ada's mother or aunt. Three near-identical surnames, no relationship between them, never addressed. The three civic workers (gauge worker, maintenance rep, allocation clerk) are walking job titles, but they're plainly meant to be, so it doesn't hurt.

### I felt something
- Page 39: "You chose safety instead of me." Felt it.
- Page 46: "He left you a choice." / "He was still a gambler." / "And he still built something worth finding." / "Also yes." Felt that too — the book letting Adrian be both things.
- Page 48: "Don't give me that much power." Best thing Ada does all book.
- Page 49: the refusal has a price — workshop sealed, clearance expiring, debt stays. I respected the book here. It didn't pay him off for being good.
- Page 53: "The water isn't." Grinned.
- Page 54: "You still thinking about leaving?" / "Every day." / "Good." Quiet, earned, worked.

### I predicted
- Mera is tied to Ada's past. Right.
- Alex refuses executive power. Right, though the "we could share it" feint briefly got me.
- The debt is not magically fixed. Right — and I was glad to be right; an erased debt would have made me put the book down on the last page out of spite.
- Adrian's death is shown or answered. Wrong — and I'm still a little annoyed about it.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
An emergency system never got switched off because the permission had no expiry date, and the answer is that nobody — not even a good kid — should get to hold the controls alone. (Third issue, third subject: water theft, then ownership, then governance.)

### Where I would have put it down
Page 50. The civic-hall procedure is where the book stops being a story and starts being a model of a process. By then I was too close to the end to actually quit, but that's where the reading became duty.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Page 54 is an overlook, an open appeal marker, and two people not deciding things for each other. It's a good ending for this book — and it closes the book. Nothing on it pulls me forward. The one thread that could (is Adrian alive?) was deliberately left to dangle, but the story just spent three issues teaching me not to expect adventure payoffs, so I don't expect one. If a next book exists, it's about an appeals process. I wish these people well and I would not buy it.

VERDICT Issue 03: put down: page 50; next issue: no

---

## Whole book

### The page that would have lost my whole class
Page 51. The climax of the book, the moment everything turns, and the big screen reads: "ALPHA ROLE: OPERATION / MONITORING / MAINTENANCE / ACCOUNTING / ALERTS." The payoff of 51 pages is a job description. Half the class is on their phones by MAINTENANCE. Page 50's "DISTRIBUTED VERIFICATION PROTOCOL" is the warm-up act that gets them reaching for their pockets.

### What I would tell a friend it was about
A kid inherits half a million credits of his missing dad's debt on his seventeenth birthday, finds out the rich cities upstairs are stealing his town's water and faking the numbers, and instead of blowing anything up he proves it with gauges, builds a home water filter with his dad's old work crew so no company can own it, gets offered emergency control of the whole system and turns it down, and the happy ending is a public complaint process that actually works. There's also a robot dog that comes apart into pieces and it's the best character. It's smarter than it sounds and slower than it should be, and it absolutely is a lesson, but the good bits — the lying gauges, the mum scene, "the water isn't" — are good enough that I finished it without hating it.

### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue
- Issue 01: Rust, debt and a number that lies — a kid proves the water's being stolen and I was genuinely in.
- Issue 02: Four strangers hand over four parts in the same scene four times while a polite man threatens everyone with paperwork, and the dog gets the only laugh.
- Issue 03: Mum left, dad's tape plays, the villain turns out to be a permission slip nobody ever cancelled, and the ending is a committee I'm glad exists and never want to read about again.
